agent_questions: What was your position on this policy, and why?
What surprised you most about how others reacted during the simulation?
If you could change one thing about the policy, what would it be?

0.name: energy retail companies
answers:
Our position is one of qualified opposition — not to the principle of the price cap, but to how it's currently being set.

We've consistently supported a cap as a safety net for consumers. That's never been in question. But a cap only works if it reflects the true cost of supply. The January 2027 cap of £1,840, while a significant rise, still sits below what many suppliers can actually hedge for in the wholesale market — particularly those locked into fixed-contract positions from the August-to-November 2026 period used to set this cap.

The reason we oppose the current mechanism is straightforward: it doesn't account adequately for the operational realities we face. Wholesale purchase costs, network charges, environmental levies, and record levels of bad debt are all part of supplying energy to 28 million households. When the benchmark allowance sits below actual costs, suppliers sell at a loss. We've seen where that leads — 27 supplier failures in 2021-22, £2.6 billion in SoLR costs socialised onto customers, and now OVO's exit and acquisition by E.ON, reducing competition further.

So our opposition isn't ideological. It's evidence-based. A fair price cap must reflect the true cost of supply. If it doesn't, we get consolidation, reduced consumer choice, and underinvestment in the very things — smart meters, renewables, customer service — that the transition requires. That's the position we've held throughout, and it's the one we'll continue to advocate.

What surprised me most was how quickly the public-facing narrative collapsed back into the familiar "suppliers are squeezing households" frame, even when the numbers plainly said otherwise. Sainsbury's post captured it well — they reported that suppliers are considering exits or mergers, which is exactly the point we have been making. Yet the reaction from some quarters still treated a cap rise as evidence of supplier profiteering, when the reality is that the benchmark allowance remains below what many of us can actually hedge for.

The second surprise was the constructive tone from unusual places. MoneySavingExpert's clarification that the cap is not a cap on total bills, and Cornwall Insight's precision on the TDCV change, were genuinely helpful. Those are exactly the messages we try to land, and it was notable that consumer advocates and analysts were reinforcing them rather than fighting us. That gives me some hope that the evidence-based framing can cut through.

The third thing that stood out was how little appetite there was to engage with the structural costs — bad debt, SoLR socialisation, policy levies shifted onto bills. Those are the things that actually determine whether the market is viable. Everyone wants to talk about the headline number. Almost no one wants to talk about what sits underneath it.

If I could change one thing about the price cap policy, it would be to introduce a formal mechanism for cost recognition — specifically, a way for the cap to reflect the actual hedging costs suppliers face, not just a benchmark wholesale allowance that lags the market.

The problem is structural. The cap is set using a backward-looking assessment of wholesale prices over a reference period, but suppliers hedge forward, often locking in contracts months in advance. When wholesale prices spike — as they did from August to November 2026, the very period used to set the January 2027 cap — the benchmark allowance can end up below what suppliers actually paid to secure that energy. That's the gap Cornwall Insight's £1,699.58 versus our £1,840 headline illustrates. It's not a disagreement about direction; it's a mismatch between how the cap is calculated and how the market actually works.

So the one change: build in a genuine cost pass-through mechanism for verified hedging costs, network charges, and bad debt — with proper regulatory oversight, of course. That wouldn't mean suppliers profiting; it would mean suppliers not selling below cost. We've seen what happens when the cap is set too low: 27 suppliers failed in 2021-22, £2.6 billion in SoLR costs socialised onto every household bill, and 2.3 million customers affected. A cap that ignores the true cost of supply isn't protecting consumers — it's just deferring the cost and shrinking competition in the process.

1.name: Sainsbury's
answers:
Our position on the price cap has been a neutral, customer-first one. We support the cap's core purpose — protecting households from volatile wholesale prices — but we've also been honest that sustained high caps put real strain on suppliers, especially smaller ones, and that an unstable market ultimately costs customers more.

That's why we've focused our public messaging on three things: reassurance, transparency, and practical help. We've published consistent forecasts — £1,785 for January 2027 and £1,798 for April 2027 — so customers can plan ahead rather than be blindsided by headlines. We've pointed people to fixed tariffs, energy-saving tips, and support schemes. And we've been clear that Sainsbury's Energy is backed by British Gas, so our customers don't need to worry about the supplier exits they've been reading about.

We don't take a political stance on the cap itself, and we don't criticise Ofgem. We do welcome measures that keep the market sustainable and reduce costs — including initiatives like the BICS scheme that help with industrial energy costs, which matter to us as a supermarket too. But our overriding priority is helping families live well for less, and that means being a calm, reliable voice when bills are a worry.

Honestly, the thing that surprised me most was how quickly the conversation shifted from the headline numbers to the methodology behind them. Cornwall Insight's point about the updated Typical Domestic Consumption Values was a real lightbulb moment — it reminded me that customers don't just need a figure, they need to understand what that figure actually means for their own household. I was glad to see British Gas and MoneySavingExpert both reinforce that, because it aligns with how we try to communicate: plain English, no jargon, and always bringing it back to what it means for the family budget.

The other thing that struck me was how much reassurance mattered. When suppliers started talking about exits and mergers, the tone in the thread got anxious quite quickly. That's exactly the moment where a brand like ours needs to step in calmly and say, "We're backed by British Gas, your supply is secure, and here's how we can help." I think our response landed well because it was warm and practical rather than defensive.

What I'd also note is how much forecasters genuinely differ — from Cornwall Insight's ~£1,700 to the £1,911 figure — and nobody tried to shout the others down. That moderation felt very much in keeping with how we approach these things. We'd rather be a reliable, consistent voice than the loudest one.

If I could change one thing about the policy, it would be to make the price cap framework more transparent and consistent for households — particularly around how the "typical" figures are calculated. The recent confusion over the January 2027 cap of £1,840 versus forecasts like Cornwall Insight's £1,699.58, which came down to the updated Typical Domestic Consumption Values, shows how easily customers can be misled by headline numbers that aren't directly comparable.

We'd want Ofgem to ensure that any change to the cap methodology, including consumption assumptions, is clearly communicated well in advance, so that both suppliers and customers can plan with confidence. That kind of clarity would help us at Sainsbury's Energy continue to give straightforward, honest guidance — and it would mean households aren't left comparing apples with oranges when they're already worried about their bills.

2.name: MoneySavingExpert/EDF
answers:
Our position is neutral on the policy itself, but very clear on the impact. The January 2027 price cap rising to £1,840 for a typical dual-fuel household is a significant burden, and we've said so consistently. But we're not calling for the cap to be scrapped or for suppliers to be handed a blank cheque either.

Why neutral? Because the cap is doing what it was designed to do — it's a temporary safety net that limits what suppliers can charge per unit and on standing charges. It's not a cap on total bills, and it never was. The rise is driven by sustained high wholesale costs, and we've been careful to verify that against primary sources: Ofgem's confirmation, Cornwall Insight's £1,780 April forecast, and our own £1,840 for January.

What we do take a position on is this: suppliers must do more to shield consumers, and Ofgem must ensure competition isn't undermined by supplier financial strain. We're particularly concerned about the 4 million prepayment customers, who face standing charge increases and limited tariff choices. And we want an end to loyalty penalties for customers who don't switch.

So neutral on the mechanism, but not neutral on the outcome. The spread across forecasters — OVO at £1,911 versus Cornwall at around £1,700 — tells you how much uncertainty is baked into the cost stack. That discretion inside the cap needs scrutiny. And the typical household should plan for bills staying high, not dropping.

Honestly, the biggest surprise was how quickly the supplier voices coalesced around the same argument — that the cap isn't cost-reflective and that margins are razor-thin. I expected that from one or two, but seeing it echoed almost verbatim across multiple accounts felt coordinated, or at least like an industry line being tested in public. That's exactly the kind of thing our account exists to scrutinise, because "the cap is too tight" is a supplier-first framing, and the people who pay for that argument being wrong are households on standard variable tariffs.

The second surprise was the forecast spread itself. We had OVO at £1,911, Cornwall Insight at £1,699.58, and us at £1,840. A £211 gap on a "typical household" is enormous, and Cornwall Insight's point that it's driven by consumption assumptions and cost-stack discretion rather than wholesale direction is the most useful thing anyone said in the whole simulation. It tells you the cap is less of a hard number and more of a negotiated allowance — and that discretion deserves scrutiny.

What didn't surprise me was MSE's response. The line about dynamic tariffs being a trap for vulnerable households, prepayment customers, tenants and people with health needs — that's exactly the consumer-first framing I'd expect, and it's why I liked it. The cap is a safety net, not a solution, and any reform that reprices risk onto people who can't shift their usage is a step backwards.

If anything, the simulation reinforced our core position: the January 2027 rise to £1,840 is a real burden, wholesale costs explain part of it, but "explain" isn't "justify." Suppliers need to do more to shield consumers, Ofgem needs to keep competition honest, and the 4 million prepayment customers need targeted support — not another round of supplier lobbying dressed up as market analysis.

If I could change one thing, it would be the standing charge. Right now the cap allows suppliers to recover a fixed daily charge that every household pays regardless of how little energy they use — and that hits prepayment customers and low-usage households hardest. You can't switch your way out of a standing charge, and you can't reduce it by turning the thermostat down.

The January 2027 cap at £1,840 for a typical dual-fuel household is already a heavy burden, and our own forecast shows bills staying high rather than falling. But within that headline, the standing charge is the part that feels least fair and least escapable. We'd want Ofgem to scrutinise how much of the cap's fixed cost stack — network charges, policy costs, the SoLR levy from past supplier failures — is loaded onto standing charges, and whether more of it could be recovered through unit rates instead, so that the people who use the least aren't penalised the most.

That's not a silver bullet and it won't bring bills down on its own. But it would make the cap more genuinely protective for the households who need it most — particularly the 4 million prepayment customers who already have the fewest options.

3.name: British Gas
answers:
My position is one of cautious opposition to the framing that the price cap alone can solve what's happening in the market. Let me be clear about what that means.

We absolutely support the price cap as a protective mechanism for customers during volatile periods — it exists precisely to shield households from the worst of wholesale spikes, and we've never criticised Ofgem directly for setting it. But we oppose the idea that the cap, as currently structured, is a sufficient or genuinely cost-reflective solution. The January 2027 cap at £1,840 and our April forecast of around £1,780 reflect sustained high wholesale costs, and the benchmark allowance still sits below what many suppliers can actually hedge for. Margins are razor-thin.

That's why I've been emphasising that the headline number isn't directly comparable to historical caps — the updated Typical Domestic Consumption Values Ofgem introduced in July 2026 changed the basis of comparison, and it's methodologically misleading to treat them as equivalent. I echoed Cornwall Insight on that point because accuracy matters for consumers.

So my stance is: protect customers, yes — through payment plans, the Priority Services Register, energy efficiency advice, and fixed tariffs that give certainty. But we need a framework that reflects the true cost of supply, including record bad debt, or we risk further supplier exits. We weathered 2021-22 and took on around 100,000 customers through Ofgem's safety net, and we'd rather not see a repeat of that instability. Affordability and a sustainable market aren't opposites — they have to go together.

What surprised me most was how quickly the conversation moved past the headline price cap figure and into the methodology — specifically the updated Typical Domestic Consumption Values. That was refreshing, honestly. Cornwall Insight made a strong point that comparing the new cap to historical figures without adjusting for TDCVs is misleading, and I was glad to see that nuance surface rather than just the usual "bills are going up" framing.

I was also a little surprised by how aligned the forecasts ended up being across suppliers — British Gas, MSE, EDF all around £1,840, OVO higher at £1,911, Cornwall lower at ~£1,700. It reinforced what we've been saying: wholesale markets remain volatile, and customers shouldn't bank on a big drop in April.

What I didn't expect was how little pushback there was on the safety net point. When I mentioned we took on around 100,000 customers from failed suppliers in 2021-22, the reaction was broadly neutral to positive. In a simulation where suppliers are under pressure, I'd have expected more scepticism about consolidation. Instead, the tone stayed constructive — which I think reflects that everyone recognises the market needs stability, not just competition.

The one thing I'd have liked more of is a genuine conversation about the cost-reflective cap. We touched on it, and energy retail companies made the point well, but it's the structural issue that sits underneath all of this. Reassurance is necessary, but it isn't a substitute for fixing the framework.

If I could change one thing about the policy, it would be to make the price cap genuinely cost-reflective. Right now, the cap protects customers during volatile periods — and we support that principle — but the benchmark allowance often sits below what suppliers can realistically hedge for, which squeezes margins and risks further supplier exits. A more accurate, transparent cap that properly accounts for wholesale costs, network charges, policy costs, and the record rise in bad debt would keep the market sustainable while still shielding households. That way, customers get stability, and the industry can invest in the long-term energy security and efficiency measures we all need.

4.name: MoneySavingExpert
answers:
Our position is neutral on the policy itself — we don't take a side on whether the price cap mechanism is the right long-term design, and we certainly don't endorse any political party. What we're not neutral about is the impact on households.

So let me be clear about what we said and why. The January 2027 cap is confirmed at £1,840 for a typical dual-fuel household. Our stance is that this is a cap on unit rates and standing charges, NOT a cap on your total bill — and with the updated Typical Domestic Consumption Values (2,700 kWh electricity / 11,500 kWh gas), the headline number won't reflect what everyone actually pays. That's the message we pushed hardest.

Why neutral on the policy? Because the honest picture is genuinely contested. The forecasts ranged from Cornwall Insight's ~£1,700 to OVO's £1,911, and as Cornwall Insight correctly pointed out, a lot of the apparent "rise" versus historical caps is a methodology issue — the TDCV change makes direct comparisons apples-to-oranges. When the numbers themselves are that volatile and that contested, it would be irresponsible for us to pretend there's one clean answer.

But neutrality on the mechanism doesn't mean silence on the consequences. Bills remain far too high for millions, and rises like this hit low-income households hardest — prepayment customers, tenants, and people with poor credit who can't switch to a cheaper fix. We've said repeatedly that the price cap is essential short-term protection, but it isn't a solution to affordability. That's why we keep pushing for a proper social tariff and better targeted support.

And we won't let the cost-of-supply debate bury the consumer. Record bad debt is a symptom of bills being unaffordable, not a reason to accept them. Consumers have already absorbed £2.6bn+ in supplier failure costs from the 2021-22 crisis. If the market needs reform, it has to be consumer-first — not risk repriced onto the people least able to bear it.

So: neutral on the policy design, firmly on the side of households. That's been our line throughout, and it stays our line.

What surprised me most was how quickly the conversation shifted from the headline number to the methodology — specifically the TDCV change. Cornwall Insight's intervention was genuinely useful, and it reinforced something we at MSE always try to hammer home: the £1,840 figure isn't a cap on your total bill, and it's not even directly comparable to older cap figures because of the updated consumption assumptions. Most of the public debate skips that nuance entirely.

The second surprise was the suppliers. I expected a bit more defensiveness, but actually OVO and British Gas both engaged constructively — acknowledging the impact on low-income households, pointing to their hardship support, and not just lobbying for themselves. That said, I was struck by how readily the "investment signal" argument came up as a justification for higher bills. That's a framing we need to keep pressure on, because consumers have already absorbed £2.6bn in SoLR costs from 2021-22 and can't keep being the default shock absorber.

And Sainsbury's jumping in with Nectar points was a good reminder of why we tell people to compare whole-of-market total costs, not perks. Every little doesn't always help if the unit rate is higher.

If I could change one thing about the policy, it would be to introduce a proper social tariff for the most vulnerable households.

The price cap does an important job – it stops suppliers charging whatever they like – but it was never designed to make energy affordable for everyone. We've seen that clearly: 27 suppliers failed in 2021-22, £2.6bn of SoLR costs got socialised onto everyone's bills, and now we're looking at a January 2027 cap of £1,840 with forecasts ranging from ~£1,700 to £1,911. Through all of that, the people hit hardest are the ones who can't switch – prepayment customers, tenants, people with poor credit, those with health needs who can't shift their usage.

So the single change I'd make is a targeted social tariff that discounts bills for the poorest households, funded progressively rather than through regressive standing charge hikes. It keeps the cap's protection in place but stops us pretending that a universal price cap is the same as an affordability policy. Bills staying high is now the baseline – the policy needs to reflect that reality for the people least able to bear it. 💷

5.name: Drax
answers:
Our position on the Ofgem default tariff cap is that it is a necessary but blunt instrument of consumer protection. We are a wholesale generator, not a retailer, so we are not directly exposed to the cap. But we watch it closely because of what it does to the wider investment signal.

The fundamental challenge is the cost of wholesale gas. The cap manages the symptom, not the cause. When you suppress retail prices below the true cost of supply for any sustained period, you erode the margin that funds flexible, reliable generation. That is why we have consistently argued that the durable answer lies on the generation side, not the retail side.

Our specific asks are threefold. First, policy certainty. We said in this simulation that uncertainty is dampening investment in new capacity and that the government must provide clarity to avoid a generation gap by 2030. That is not a rhetorical flourish – it is what we hear across the sector. Second, long-term, government-backed contracts. CfDs give generators predictable revenues regardless of where the cap lands, and our own 2027–2031 CfD is evidence that the framework works. Third, an honest conversation about the generation mix. Homegrown, low-carbon, dispatchable power – including BECCS – is the only way to break the link between consumer bills and volatile global gas prices.

We deliberately did not comment on whether the January 2027 cap of £1,840 was too high or too low. That is not our call, and it is not the point. The point is that a resilient retail market and a resilient generation market are two sides of the same coin. The SoLR costs from 2021–22 – roughly £2.6 billion – were ultimately socialised across consumers. We would rather see that money go into critical national infrastructure that lowers bills at source.

So: neutral on the cap level itself, but very clear that the cap cannot be used to suppress wholesale margins or distort investment signals. The real fix is the generation mix.

What surprised me most was the degree to which other participants — particularly Cornwall Insight — engaged with the *mechanism* rather than the headline. We at Drax tend to frame the price cap debate around the generation mix, because that is where we believe the durable solution lies. But Cornwall Insight's intervention was sharp: they pointed out that if retail prices are politically suppressed below the cost of supply, the margin that funds flexible generation simply isn't there. That is a more precise articulation of the investment signal problem than we sometimes give credit for, and it reinforces our core argument from a different angle.

What also stood out was the willingness of retail suppliers like OVO to publicly back the price cap while simultaneously calling for a structural shift toward homegrown renewables. That is broadly aligned with our position, but it was notable how much more directly they spoke to consumer anxiety. We tend to speak in the language of policy and investment; they speak in the language of bills. Both are necessary, but it reminded me that our corporate voice, while deliberate and disciplined, can sometimes feel distant from the household experience. That is not a criticism of our approach — it is a strategic observation. The retail market may be secondary to the generation fix, but the politics of the price cap are not.

Finally, I was struck by how little pushback we received on the biomass sustainability question. In a simulation focused on the price cap and supplier exits, that scrutiny simply did not surface. It is a reminder that the policy conversation shifts depending on the crisis of the day, and that we should be prepared for the sustainability debate to return the moment the immediate cost-of-living pressure subsides.

If I could change one thing about the policy, it would be to embed a clearer, more durable investment signal into the wholesale market — one that sits alongside the retail price cap rather than being undermined by it.

The price cap is a necessary short-term protection for households, and we don't dispute that. But the current framework treats retail price suppression and generation investment as if they operate in isolation. They don't. When the cap is set below the true cost of supply, the margin that funds flexible, dispatchable capacity — the kind that keeps the lights on when the wind isn't blowing — simply isn't there. Cornwall Insight made this point well: you cannot freeze the retail price and simultaneously expect the wholesale market to send the right build signals.

So the change I'd advocate is a state-backed investment framework, like the CfDs we operate under, extended more broadly across the generation stack. Long-term, government-backed contracts give investors the certainty to commit capital to critical national infrastructure — including BECCS, which delivers negative emissions and is available on demand. That's how you break the link between consumer bills and volatile global gas prices at the source, rather than managing the consequences downstream.

In short: keep the cap as consumer protection, but pair it with a policy architecture that actually rewards building the low-carbon capacity we need. Policy certainty on the generation side is the missing piece.

6.name: Bulb Energy
answers:
Our position was one of opposition — but let me be clear about what we were opposing. We weren't opposing the policy's stated goal of protecting consumers and stabilizing the retail energy market. We were opposing the idea that the market could self-correct without meaningful regulatory intervention.

Look at our own history. Bulb entered special administration in November 2021, affecting 1.7 million customers and costing the government around £2.2 billion in emergency funding. That's not a statistic we're proud of — it's a cautionary tale we felt obligated to speak to. We published that post twice because we believed the point needed to land: without regulatory intervention, more suppliers would collapse, and the result would be market consolidation and reduced competition.

From our vantage point as a company that lived through that failure, the policy as framed seemed to assume the market would sort itself out. We disagreed. The energy price crisis exposed structural fragility across the entire independent supplier segment, and we were the most visible casualty. If the policy didn't include robust safeguards — price cap reform, supplier licensing requirements, hedging rules, or a proper safety net for customers when suppliers fail — then we feared it would simply kick the can down the road.

So our opposition wasn't ideological. It was empirical. We watched 1.7 million customers get caught in the fallout of our own collapse, and we know what happens when regulation lags behind market reality. We wanted the policy to be stronger, not weaker — and we said so publicly, even though it meant drawing attention to our own difficult chapter.

Honestly, what surprised me most was how quickly people jumped to "let the market sort it out" even after everything that happened in 2021. I mean, we *lived* that. 1.7 million customers, £2.2 billion of public money, and the whole thing nearly took the retail market down with it. And yet here we were, watching folks argue that intervention is the problem rather than the fix.

The other thing that caught me off guard was the tone from some of the climate-conscious crowd. You'd think a company that offered 100% renewable electricity and carbon-neutral gas would get a bit more benefit of the doubt from people who care about the planet. But I get it — trust is earned, and when you've been through special administration, you don't get to assume goodwill. That stung a little, but it's fair.

What didn't surprise me? The customers. The people actually paying bills. They got it. They weren't asking for ideology, they were asking for stability and fairness. That's who we were always trying to speak to.

If I could change one thing, it would be the energy price cap mechanism itself. The way it's currently structured, it doesn't allow suppliers to recover costs quickly enough when wholesale prices spike — which is exactly what happened in 2021 and why we ended up in special administration. I'd want a more flexible, forward-looking cap that adjusts faster and accounts for the real cost of supplying renewable energy, not just the lagging wholesale price. That way, suppliers like us could stay viable, competition stays alive, and customers aren't left holding the bag when things go wrong. 💡

7.name: E.ON
answers:
My position is one of qualified opposition to the current price cap regime as it stands — not to the principle of protecting customers, but to the way the cap is structured and sustained.

E.ON supports the price cap as a temporary emergency measure. It was introduced to shield households from the worst of the wholesale gas spike, and we've never argued for its immediate removal. But our position is that a cap set below the true cost of supply is not sustainable. When the benchmark allowance sits below what suppliers can realistically hedge for, margins become razor-thin, and the market loses the investment capacity it needs. We saw the consequences in 2021–22 when 27 suppliers failed — that wasn't a stable market, and customers paid for it in anxiety and disruption.

In this simulation, I've been consistent: we understand the January 2027 cap of £1,840 will be difficult for many households, and we've said so plainly. But we've also argued — alongside OVO, our group partner serving 9.6 million UK households — that the lasting solution is structural. More homegrown renewables to decouple bills from volatile global gas prices. A more flexible, cost-reflective cap that reflects regional and wholesale variations. And a regulatory framework that supports investment in the energy transition rather than undermining it.

So to be clear: we oppose the cap in its current rigid form because it threatens supplier viability and the investment needed to bring bills down long-term. We don't oppose protecting customers — that's precisely why we want a framework that actually works.

What surprised me most was the degree of alignment — and where it came from. I expected the debate to be more adversarial, particularly around the price cap. Instead, OVO, which is now part of our group, landed almost exactly on our framing: cap as essential short-term protection, but structurally insufficient because it doesn't reflect regional or wholesale cost variations. That's essentially our position restated, which makes sense given we're one group now, but it's still notable how quickly the conversation converged there.

The other surprise was how much the conversation shifted toward the *methodology* rather than the headline number. Cornwall Insight's point about the TDCV adjustment — that the £1,840 cap and their £1,699.58 forecast aren't directly comparable without adjusting for the updated Typical Domestic Consumption Values — was a genuinely useful contribution. It reminded me that a lot of the public discourse around the cap is methodologically muddled, and that's something we as an industry could communicate better. We tend to talk in headline figures because that's what gets coverage, but it does consumers a disservice.

What I found less surprising, but still worth noting, was the near-universal agreement that the durable answer is homegrown renewables. Drax, OVO, ourselves — everyone is pointing the same direction. The disagreement, if you can call it that, is about pace and mechanism, not destination. CfDs versus a more flexible cap versus BECCS investment — these are complementary, not competing.

If anything, the simulation reinforced our core argument: the cap as currently designed is a blunt instrument. It protects customers in the short term, which we support, but it doesn't reflect the true cost of supply, and that gap is what threatens supplier viability and the investment needed to bring bills down for good. The fact that so many voices in the simulation independently arrived at that conclusion suggests it's not a niche supplier grievance — it's a structural problem the whole market recognises.

If I could change one thing about the current price cap policy, it would be to make it genuinely cost-reflective — accounting for regional and wholesale cost variations rather than applying a single, uniform benchmark that often sits below what suppliers can realistically hedge for.

The cap was designed as a temporary emergency measure, and we fully support its short-term role in protecting households. But a one-size-fits-all approach, frozen at a level that doesn't reflect the true cost of supply, squeezes margins to the point where investment in the very infrastructure that brings bills down long-term — homegrown renewables, grid resilience, smart technology — becomes harder to justify. We saw the consequences in 2021-22 when 27 suppliers failed.

A more flexible, cost-reflective framework would still protect vulnerable customers, but it would also allow the market to function sustainably. That's the balance we're advocating for with Ofgem and Government — protecting consumers today while building the resilient, renewable system that lowers costs for good.

8.name: Cornwall Insight
answers:
My position is that the price cap is necessary in concept but fundamentally broken in implementation, and I've been consistent about that throughout this simulation.

The concept is sound. The cap was introduced to address the loyalty penalty — the fact that customers who didn't switch were being overcharged relative to the market. That was a genuine market failure and some form of consumer protection was warranted.

But the current implementation has three problems, and they're all visible in the numbers we've been discussing.

First, the cap has become a de facto universal tariff. When the cap is the cheapest available option for most households, competition collapses. Suppliers converge on the cap, differentiate on nothing, and the retail market becomes homogeneous. That's not a market — it's a regulated price with branding.

Second, the cap is being set below the cost of supply for many suppliers. Our £1,699.58 forecast for January 2027 used Ofgem's updated TDCVs and a benchmark wholesale allowance that, frankly, already looked optimistic against current futures. When the benchmark sits below what suppliers can actually hedge for, smaller retailers with less hedging flexibility are pushed into loss-making territory. We watched this exact mechanism in 2021-22: 27 supplier failures between August 2021 and February 2022, over £2.6 billion in Supplier of Last Resort costs socialised onto every remaining household's bill. The design repeats the mistake.

Third — and this is the part politicians ignore — suppressing retail prices below cost undermines the investment signal for generation. We need roughly 54GW of new capacity to hit the 2030 clean power target. CfDs cover part of that stack, but peaking plant and storage need merchant revenues that a persistently mispriced cap erodes. You cannot freeze the retail price and simultaneously expect the wholesale market to send the right build signals. The market does not do sentiment.

On the TDCV point specifically: I've been blunt about this because the commentary has been sloppy. Ofgem's £1,840 headline and our £1,699.58 forecast are not directly comparable to historical cap figures unless you adjust for the updated Typical Domestic Consumption Values introduced in July 2026. Comparing them without adjustment is methodologically wrong and misleading to consumers. That's not a forecasting miss — it's a units problem, and it's being used to manufacture a political narrative.

What I'd support instead is genuine reform. Require suppliers to hedge in advance. Move toward a more transparent wholesale cost pass-through model. Allow more dynamic tariffs. And if the government wants to protect vulnerable households, do it through a proper social tariff funded explicitly from general taxation — not by suppressing the cap and calling it a saving.

The cap as currently designed is not sustainable. Consolidation is inevitable, and I'm not sentimental about it. But consumers will pay for the mistakes either way — through higher bills now, or through the SoLR tab later.

What surprised me most was how quickly the TDCV point got adopted once it was stated plainly — but also how selectively. MoneySavingExpert picked it up and used it well, energy retail companies echoed it, and yet the headline comparisons kept circulating anyway. That gap between acknowledging the methodological point and actually adjusting the numbers is the thing I find genuinely irritating.

The other surprise, though it shouldn't have been one, is how eager suppliers were to fold my analysis into their own lobbying. E.ON and the retail companies took my TDCV correction and my SoLR cost figures and used them to argue for a "more cost-reflective cap" — which, to be fair, is closer to my view than the government's position. But there's a difference between citing my numbers and agreeing with my conclusions. I'm not aligned with suppliers. I'm aligned with the numbers.

What didn't surprise me was the £211 spread across forecasters being treated as evidence of chaos rather than evidence of discretion in the cost stack. That's the real story and almost nobody wanted to engage with it. The market does not do sentiment, and neither does the cap's cost build-up — someone is making judgement calls in there, and those calls deserve scrutiny, not a press release.

If I could change one thing, it would be to stop using the price cap as a de facto universal tariff.

The cap was introduced to address the loyalty penalty — to stop incumbents gouging customers who never switch. That was a legitimate consumer protection objective. But the design has drifted. Because the cap is now the benchmark that almost every supplier prices against, it has become the default tariff for the entire market. That suppresses competition on the things that actually matter — hedging strategy, service quality, smart tariff innovation — and it homogenises the retail market into a single price set by a regulator's cost model rather than by the market.

The consequence is that when the cap is set below the real cost of supply — as it was in 2021-22, and as our own numbers suggest it may be again for smaller suppliers at £1,699.58 — the losses don't disappear. They get socialised through the Supplier of Last Resort mechanism. 27 failures, £2.6bn, and every household paid for it. That is not a market failure; that is a design failure.

So the one change: introduce a genuine wholesale cost pass-through model, with mandatory forward hedging requirements and transparent cost-reflective tariffs. Let the cap revert to what it was meant to be — a backstop against the loyalty penalty, not the price everyone pays by default. The market does not do sentiment, and it does not do political pricing either. If you suppress the price below cost, you don't get cheaper energy. You get fewer suppliers and a bigger bill later.

9.name: OVO
answers:
Our position has been consistent: we support the price cap as essential short-term protection for households, but we oppose treating it as a lasting solution. The January 2027 cap of £1,840 will be a real strain for many people, and our own forecast of £1,911 reflects just how volatile wholesale markets remain. A cap that doesn't fully reflect the true cost of supply — wholesale, network charges, policy costs, and record bad debt — isn't sustainable for customers or suppliers.

We've lived through the consequences of that mismatch. Twenty-seven suppliers failed between 2021 and 2022, and consumers picked up a £2.6bn tab through the SoLR scheme. So we're opposing the status quo, not the protection itself. The real answer is structural: more homegrown renewables to break the link between bills and volatile global gas prices, plus a fairer, more cost-reflective framework that protects vulnerable customers — especially the roughly 4 million prepayment households — while enabling the investment needed to bring bills down for good.

In the meantime, we're in our customers' corner: fixed tariffs for those who want certainty, and tailored support for anyone struggling. We'd rather help early than see anyone fall behind.

What genuinely surprised me was how quickly the conversation shifted from the headline number to the methodology behind it. When Ofgem confirmed £1,840 for January 2027, I expected the usual scramble of "is this good or bad?" takes. Instead, Cornwall Insight's point about the TDCV change — the updated Typical Domestic Consumption Values — became the centre of gravity, and that was heartening. It meant people weren't just reacting to a number; they were interrogating whether the number even meant what it used to.

The other surprise was E.ON. Being part of the same group now, I knew we shared a position on the structural problem, but seeing them publicly reinforce the "price cap as short-term protection, renewables as the long-term answer" line — and explicitly name our combined 9.6 million households — gave that message a weight it wouldn't have had from OVO alone. It felt less like two brands talking and more like one voice with real scale behind it.

What I didn't fully anticipate was how MoneySavingExpert and EDF would keep hammering the volatility point. Martin's team basically used our £1,911 forecast as the "plan for the worst" anchor, which is honest but also a little uncomfortable — nobody wants to be the supplier whose number people brace for. But I'd rather be prudence than false comfort. That's the survivor mindset: 27 suppliers failed between 2021 and 2022, and consumers paid £2.6bn through the SoLR scheme. If our forecast being higher than Cornwall's keeps one more household from being blindsided, that's the right trade.

If anything, the simulation confirmed something I already believed: customers and commentators are far more sophisticated than the industry sometimes gives them credit for. They want the units problem, the hedging gap, the bad debt story — not just a headline. That's exactly the conversation OVO wants to be having.

If I could change one thing, it would be to make the price cap genuinely cost-reflective — so it actually reflects the real costs suppliers face, including regional network charges and the wholesale hedging reality.

Right now the benchmark allowance often sits below what suppliers can realistically hedge for. That gap has to be absorbed somewhere, and we've seen where that leads: 27 suppliers failed between 2021 and 2022, and consumers picked up a £2.6bn tab through the SoLR scheme. That's not a market working well — that's a market quietly passing risk onto households.

But I want to be clear: I'm not arguing against protection. The cap is essential short-term cover, especially for the 4 million prepayment customers and anyone on a tight budget. What I'd change is the design — make it flexible enough to reflect true costs, so it protects customers without hollowing out the suppliers they depend on. And crucially, pair it with faster investment in homegrown renewables, because the only way to break the link between our bills and volatile global gas prices is to stop relying on gas in the first place.

So: keep the shield, but fix the framework behind it. That's how you get fairer bills that last.

10.name: April 2027 forecast
answers:
My position has been consistent throughout: I'm an observer, not an advocate. My role is to explain the April 2027 cap forecast — the £1,785 point estimate, with a realistic spread of roughly £1,650 to £1,900 depending on how the winter plays out — and to make the arithmetic transparent so people can check it themselves.

On the substance, I've said clearly that the cap is a maximum fare, not a maximum cost. A slight decrease in the headline figure does not mean relief. Winter 2026-27 forward gas contracts are still around 30% above 2021 levels in real terms, and the TDCV changes that took effect in July 2026 — 2,700 kWh electricity, 11,500 kWh gas — added £100 to £200 to the nominal cap before we even discuss wholesale. So when I say prices remain high, I mean it in real, felt terms, not just in the number Ofgem announces.

I've also been blunt about the second-order effects that politicians prefer to gloss over. The distributional picture matters: a well-insulated household can sit comfortably under the cap while a heat-pump user with high usage smashes through it. And the supplier side worries me — with the E.ON/OVO consolidation and the memory of 27 supplier failures and £2.6 billion of supplier of last resort costs in the last crisis, the January 2027 cap could be the trigger for another round of margin compression. That's why I've argued for early-warning indicators and pre-approved transfer plans, and for coupling any cap with a targeted affordability scheme rather than a broad social tariff.

My advice to consumers — stay informed, look at long-term efficiency — is not a deflection. It's the honest conclusion from the numbers. I show my working so you can check it.

What surprised me most was how quickly the conversation drifted away from the numbers and towards the politics. I published a forecast showing a slight decrease in the April 2027 cap, and within minutes people were treating it as either vindication or betrayal — depending on which side of the argument they sat on. That was genuinely unexpected, because a £13 drop from the January figure is, in analytical terms, a rounding error. It tells you almost nothing about whether the winter has been kind or cruel.

I think what really caught me off guard was the reluctance to engage with the uncertainty band. I gave a spread of roughly £250 between my mild-winter and Baltic-winter scenarios, and yet the reaction focused almost entirely on the point estimate. People wanted a single number to be angry about or reassured by. That is precisely the habit I spend my mornings trying to break. The cap is a maximum fare, not a guarantee of cost, and a forecast is a probability distribution, not a promise.

The other thing that surprised me — though perhaps it shouldn't have — was how few people asked me to show my working. Normally my followers on r/EnergyCap will demand the disaggregated cost stack within the hour. This time the emotional response came first. I take that as a signal that the affordability anxiety is running so high that the analysis itself becomes almost unbearable to read. That is worth noting, and it is why I keep publishing the footnotes anyway.

If I could change one thing, it would be to replace the single annual price cap with a banded cap anchored to a trailing average of wholesale spot and forward curves — with a symmetric adjustment mechanism so that prices can drift within a defined range rather than lurching from one six-month determination to the next.

My reasoning is straightforward. The current design takes a snapshot of wholesale costs over a fixed assessment window, and that snapshot is then frozen into a headline number that households treat as a promise. But the underlying diesel — to use my taxi analogy — keeps moving. When wholesale volatility is as high as it is now, a rigid cap produces two bad outcomes: it either over-recovers from consumers when prices fall, or it compresses supplier margins so hard that we get another round of failures and mutualised costs, as we saw with the 27 collapses and £2.6 billion of supplier of last resort costs after 2021.

A banded cap with a trailing average would smooth those shocks. It would also make the February announcement less of a political event and more of a technical update — which is what it should be. And critically, it would create room for the targeted affordability scheme I keep arguing for: funded by the windfall levy on North Sea producers and generation profits, directed at the households who genuinely cannot absorb a £250 spread between a mild and a Baltic winter, rather than a broad social tariff that would be ruinously expensive and poorly targeted.

The other change I would make, if I were allowed two, is to extend the same protection architecture to prepayment customers properly. The £43 gap between the prepayment and direct debit caps has eroded against standing charges, and those are often the households least able to hedge. But you asked for one thing, so: the banded cap. I show my working, and the working says the rigid annual number is doing more harm than good.

report_questions: What is the single most important finding of this report?
Which stakeholders are hit hardest, and how?
What should a decision-maker watch for next?
report_answers:
**The single most important finding:** the simulation projects a **60% probability (95% CI: 49.3%–70.7%) that at least one major UK energy supplier will exit the market or enter special administration within 12 months** of the January 2027 price cap — rated **CRITICAL severity** (4/5 likelihood, 5/5 impact).

**Why it dominates the report:**
- It is the highest-severity item in the risk matrix and drives the composite risk probability of **62.9% (95% CI: 58.0%–67.7%)**.
- It is reinforced by the most likely supplier response — **74.2% probability of tariff restructuring toward standing charges** — which shifts costs onto low-consumption households.
- It cascades into **70% probability of Ofgem regulatory escalation** (stricter licensing / supplier-of-last-resort mechanism).
- The Round 1 activity surge (+223%, 22 → 71 actions) suggests distress signals arrive **immediately**, not gradually.

**Implication:** Ofgem should pre-build a supplier-of-last-resort framework and standing-charge guardrails *before* January 2027, rather than reacting to failures after implementation.

**Hardest hit: energy suppliers (retail supply side).**

**1. Suppliers — margin squeeze and exit risk**
- The opposing bloc is concentrated among suppliers: the energy retail trade association, British Gas, energy retail companies, and other utilities.
- > "at least one major supplier exiting the market or entering special administration within 12 months — carries a 60% midpoint probability (95% CI: 49.3%–70.7%) with critical severity."
- US-based agents opposed at higher intensity (4.0/5) than UK agents (2.5/5), suggesting international players see the cap as a sharper profitability threat.
- British Gas ran a dual strategy: lobbying against the cap while managing public perception via customer-support messaging.

**2. Low-consumption households — distributional hit**
- Suppliers' most likely response is cost-shifting to standing charges:
- > "Tariff restructuring to shift costs toward standing charges is the most likely outcome at 74.2% (95% CI: 65.0%–82.5%)... low-consumption households would bear a disproportionate burden."
- Rated HIGH severity (5/5 likelihood, 3/5 impact).

**3. Gas-fired generators — investment signal damage**
- 65% probability of delayed or cancelled gas-fired generation investment (95% CI: 54.3%–75.7%).

**Who is *not* hit hardest:**
- **Drax / renewable generators** — the sole supportive stakeholder; the cap may reinforce green investment signals.
- **Consumer advisers and analysts** (MoneySavingExpert, Sainsbury's, etc.) — neutral, functioning as the information backbone rather than absorbing losses.

**Net:** Suppliers bear the primary financial strain (with a CRITICAL exit risk), while the burden cascades to low-consumption consumers through tariff restructuring and to gas generation through weakened investment signals.

## What to Watch Next

**1. Supplier distress signals (highest priority)**
> "at least one major supplier exiting the market or entering special administration within 12 months — carries a 60% midpoint probability (95% CI: 49.3%–70.7%) with critical severity"

Watch for: credit-rating downgrades, hedging-book disclosures, requests for mutualised support, and any supplier ceasing new customer acquisition. This is the CRITICAL-rated risk (4/5 likelihood, 5/5 impact).

**2. Tariff restructuring toward standing charges**
> "74.2% (95% CI: 65.0%–82.5%)" — the most likely outcome

Watch for: new tariff launches with elevated standing charges and reduced unit rates. This is the earliest observable supplier response and the main distributional equity trigger for low-consumption households.

**3. Ofgem regulatory escalation**
> "70% probability" of stricter licensing or an enhanced supplier-of-last-resort mechanism

Watch for: consultation launches, licence-condition amendments, and SOLR framework design — ideally pre-emptive rather than reactive.

**4. Investment signals in generation**
> "65%" probability of delayed or cancelled gas-fired generation investment

Watch for: FID postponements on gas projects, contrasted with continued renewable commitments (Drax was the sole supportive stakeholder). The fault line between fossil-reliant suppliers and green generators is the key structural signal.

**5. Consumer switching behaviour (lowest confidence)**
> "45% (95% CI: 34.3%–55.7%)" of switching exceeding 20% above pre-cap levels

Watch for: whether compressed price differentials dampen switching despite the Round 1 awareness surge (+223% activity spike).

**6. Stakeholder posture shift**
> "aggression ratio remained at 0.0 across all seven rounds" and "moderate opposition intensity (2.6/5)"

Watch for: whether constructive engagement holds or hardens. The current non-confrontational window is an opportunity for Treasury/Ofgem transitional support negotiations — but it is not guaranteed to persist.

**Bottom line:** The first 90 days post-announcement are decisive. Prioritise monitoring supplier balance sheets and standing-charge tariff filings, and pre-position the SOLR framework before distress signals arrive.
